name: Andean peoples of north-west Argentina (Omaguaca, Ocloya, Tastil, Tonokoté, Sanavirones, Atacameño)
summary: A set of separate Andean and valley peoples of what is now north-west Argentina, grouped here only because they share a region and an entry-level source list; this is a stub to be improved.

location.value: Valleys and ravines of north-west Argentina in the provinces of Salta, Tucumán, Catamarca, La Rioja and San Juan (the Calchaquí valleys), and the Puna and Quebrada of Jujuy, plus the plains of Santiago del Estero.
location.source: Billiken: Diaguitas (search excerpt); Argentina photo gallery blog: first peoples of the northwest (search excerpt)

economicBase.value: Sedentary farming: the Tonocoté were mainly farmers between the Dulce and Salado rivers.
economicBase.source: Argentina photo gallery blog: first peoples of the northwest (search excerpt)

governmentType.value: No single state. Many separate peoples: the Argentine lists name Omaguaca, Ocloya, Tastil, Tonokoté, Sanavirones, Diaguita (Calchaquí and Cacano) and Kolla-Atacameño. Collective names such as Diaguita and Calchaquí come from colonial sources.
governmentType.source: Lifeder: Los 38 pueblos originarios de Argentina (search excerpt); Penn DIA maps of Argentine peoples, from INAI (search excerpts)

majorWars.value: The Calchaquí valley held out against the Spanish invasion for over 160 years; the first war ran from 1534 to 1565 under a leader the source calls Juan Calchaquí. The Omaguaca resisted both Incas and Spaniards.
majorWars.source: CORE: Uturunku Achachi 2013 (search excerpt); Argentina photo gallery blog: first peoples of the northwest (search excerpt)

alliancesRivals.value: Tonocoté land was limited by the Sanavirones to the south, the Calchaquíes to the west, and the warlike Lule to the north and east.
alliancesRivals.source: Argentina photo gallery blog: first peoples of the northwest (search excerpt)

languageWriting.value: Cacán, the Diaguita language, died out over 200 years ago; it survives only in place-names such as Payogasta.

sharedIdentity.value: The name Diaguita is thought to be Quechua with Aymara roots, given by the Inca, and means 'serrano' (highlander); the name Calchaquí came from early chronicles.

neighbours.value: The Inca (Collasuyo) to the north; Lule, Vilela and Sanavirones around the plains; Atacameño and Diaguita groups across the Andes in Chile.
neighbours.source: Argentina photo gallery blog: first peoples of the northwest (search excerpt); Penn DIA maps of Argentine peoples, from INAI (search excerpts)

sources.value: Search excerpts only (no full page read): Lifeder, Penn DIA/INAI peoples lists, Billiken, a blog on north-west peoples and a CORE article; 17 Nov 2026. These lists give names and places but little on how each people lived before 1492, so most items are empty.

overallCertainty.value: Weak. Names come from colonial sources and modern census lists; the 1492 map labels may stand for separate peoples, so a full entry needs primary reading.
overallCertainty.source: Lifeder: Los 38 pueblos originarios de Argentina (search excerpt)
